blocks.x: This is an interview being recorded in the Seminar Room 2 of the Howard-Chilton Memorial Library at Tulane University. The day is August 31, 1962. My name is Paul Crawford and I'll ask the interviewer and the interviewee to introduce themselves.
My name is William R. Hogan and I'm here mostly listening to Bill Russell.

This is Bill Russell. I'll start in a little bit with my life since they wanted to know a few of the early facts. I was born 1905, February the 26th, in a small town up on the Mississippi, Canton, Missouri, about 150 miles north of St. Louis. There was little music in the town, although I remember as early as I can remember hearing different orchestras. Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland

At the end of the previous tape, Mr. Russell was relating the fact that he moved to New Orleans, where he ran a record shop in the French Quarter, which I know was a rendezvous of all sorts of musicians from not only this part of the world, but from abroad. He taught music in what, in some, the Golden Gate?
No, it's called the Educational Gateways.
Educational Gateways.

A private school that specialized in music, and I also even taught speed reading and remedial reading out there, too, when I first started. But mostly, my interest naturally was music, but different instruments, string, wind, anything that was needed. It was private lessons, and they also had classwork in theory, of course.

Then since 1958, he has been connected with the Archive of New Orleans Jazz at Tulane University as curator, and one of his chief contributions has been interviewing a great many musicians on tape and preparing notes on this material. And he's now in the position of having to go back to Missouri to take care of his invalid mother, and that's one of the reasons we're getting the interview before he leaves. Mr. Russell, were you ever married?
No.
Never married?

Never had time. You're too busy running around collecting. No wife would ever put up the way I move around from one place to another and spend my time on music records or anything that came into my head that way I'd get.
Do you have any personal points of view that might, might have one that was interested in you that you'd like to express before we go into these musicians?
No, I can't really think of anything.
Don't you think you've really spent your life trying to sell New Orleans music?
Well, not.
I don't mean sell it. I mean to interest people in it, because it really means a great deal to you.
Yes, I've always loved the music so much, and naturally I've always talked about the musicians as being the greatest music I've heard.
You really believe that?
Yes.
Now you're talking about New Orleans.

Yeah, that's right. I always tell people like Bunk Johnson, I studied with some other very great musicians, I will say Arnold Schoenberg, whom some people consider as at least one of the two or three greatest modern composers, and other, not to knock any of the classical musicians, but as I always say, Bunk had more music in him, and I learned more from him about music, and what music can do for people, and what its real place is in life, and I ever did before.
You mean he expressed this in his own personality as well as in his music?
Yes, and in his views and talking about it. He was intelligent enough to talk about music too. I mean he had some wonderful ideas on music and life in general.
Now during all this, you never made a tremendous amount of money at any point, did you?

No, I always made enough to eat on, and that's about all I ever cared for. I liked to have a few things. I mean the records I picked up, which would be invaluable to me, and other people too, which I wouldn't sell mostly at any price sometime when I was offered for them, even if I didn't have money, but I got them very cheaply. During the Depression you could pick those, anything up to sheet music or anything else that I was interested in. I worked hard for it, but at least it came at a very low price, so I never needed much money fortunately in the things I was doing.
You want to talk about some of these musicians you've encountered in the course of your career now?

Yes, I might talk a little bit. I happened to pick up an old big box at home I have called Notes, and I dug out a few of the notebooks and other things. One package of notes envelope called Jazzmen material that we collected in 1938 when we were working on Jazzmen. Unfortunately then, we not only didn't have tape recording, we didn't have any other recorders. Nobody was hardly recording interviews. When I started out about that time, they were using mostly aluminum blanks there for a while. You had to play with wooden needles. Anyway, we just would go into someone's home and talk to them. I didn't know shorthand. I'd just copy down a word here and there as much as I could and try to remember. I had a pretty good memory in those days. This was in the middle 30s? In 1938 this was actually. Before that I'd gone to see people like Jimmy Noon, Johnny Dodds, and Armstrong, and met a few of my favorite New Orleans musicians. I didn't talk to them in any systematic way about their life, but I would just try to get to be friends and understand the music and understand them better. That is, get to know them better, you might say. And they were very, I found that true, that always the New Orleans musicians, the colored or white or any of them from here, have always been much more friendly. After talking to the New York musicians, for instance, who I'm not trying to knock either, but there's something cold or commercial about most of them, even the jazz musicians. And so many people that come down here, they can't believe it, that they can walk in anybody's home here and get a nice reception. They'll usually make them stay for dinner. Give them some gumbo. Yeah, give them gumbo and they'll talk to them up there. They'll, they try to get rid of them. Say the 52nd, what used to be the 52nd Street crowd or down in the village, I'm not trying to mention any names, but say the usual ones that used to play at Nick's or Eddie Conlon's. I don't mean Eddie Conlon, he's a very good talker and quite a friendly guy, but I mean the type of musicians, the so-called Dixieland musicians in New York who came mostly from the north up there, they, they're not quite that friendly. And it's so easy to meet them here in Chicago, the New Orleans musicians that were up there too, like say Johnny Dodds and Baby and any of the fellows that you know.
How do you explain that?

I don't know. It's something about the city. It's something about the music maybe that makes them better people. There's a friend of mine, Ralph Collins, always had that theory too. He said he wanted to really test it when he got to New Orleans. He figured a good guy is going to be a good musician. The good musicians are good guys and that's, it's almost always that way. They're not perfect either. Everybody has plenty of faults, but I mean they're not small people or crooks or all that. I mean they're, they're nice, nice people.
Most of them, a lot of them have always been very friendly.
So we figure maybe the music does something for them. I don't know.
Well, you think that maybe it has something to do with the general environment.

Or else it's the type of people that, for one thing, one of the great principles which you can't really overemphasize in New Orleans music, in the jazz, is the working together. The way they can work together. They're all there to help one another, as they say. They'll, they're not there to steal the spotlight. They're always there trying to help somebody misses a note or they can see they're falling down on their part. They'll put in notes that'll fill in or they'll, I mean, it's not quite that simple, but I mean it's that spirit that the musicians do work together. That's one of the main principles that's made New Orleans music what it is. Everybody talks about the ensemble style as opposed to solo style, but that's a part of it, that working together and the friendly spirit. And yet some of the bands sometimes can get in sort of fights too. You'll find a lot of that goes on even here, but not as much as other, other places. You mean within the band? Within the band. Not nearly as much. And they're a good band that really is playing well together there. As Baby Dodd says, you have to be friendly, you have to be happy. Incidentally, that's in a little drum book. Some of that's in his autobiography too. But I have a little drum book which I hope someday will be published, maybe as a part of a bigger book. I started this work in Chicago of interviewing some of what I consider the outstanding New Orleans musicians on each instrument. To find out what their part in the band is. What they, not necessarily instruction to younger players, but also that would be of value to younger players coming up that wanted to take up New Orleans style. What they have to do, what they have to learn to play the New Orleans style. So up there in Chicago I'd interviewed Baby Dodds quite a few interviews, as well as some of his music, demonstrating the drums and different traps as they call them. Also, Omer Simeon, who was certainly one of the outstanding New Orleans clarinetists, although he didn't play hardly, I guess, at all down here. But he was a member of Jelly Rolls band up there, and Jelly considered him the greatest clarinetist he'd ever worked with.
He was my favorite of all of them on my own record.

And then also, not that I was just trying to pick Jelly's favorite musicians, but Roy Palmer, whom Jelly also considered the best trombonist. Who had only recorded one very early date with Jelly on an old autograph session. But I had a good interview with him. And also Natty Dominick, who maybe wasn't one of the two or three greatest all-time trumpet players, but certainly had a wonderful rhythmic driving style. One of the choice men as far as personally a wonderful fellow.
Are you going to talk about your personal contact with Jelly?

Yes, I might say, let me finish up first about the notes for jazz men in general. We, one thing I did was to go to the Chicago Defender, the Negro newspaper on the south side, and went through their old files from 1917 on. And I only worked there a couple of days. And I had very sketchy notes, which I wish had been much fuller, because they destroyed those files up to 1923 later. And they began with 1923 to put them on microfilm, which are still available.
The early ones are not available?

No, at best. And also, I have a note here I noticed right here in front of me. I think the 1919 and 1920 files were missing, even in 1938 when I went there, in December of 1938. But I have some of these notes, which I'll go over, and might be able to enlarge a little bit on them. These are rather sketchy. Put on ahead. I mean, I'll send them down to Missouri. I see. Because it's a job that's going to take hours and days to go over that. And I'll copy it out, and it'll have to be by longhand, and I'll send a carbon copy down, and I'll make it at the same time. Maybe months before you get it, but a note here to Mrs. Rankin or whoever hears this later. If you don't get that, don't give up, but keep reminding me occasionally when you write. And some other notes in the Jazzmen envelope, which I'll send, are a little sketch of the New Orleans Rhythm Kings, some concerts, at least one concert they gave in 37, I noticed was prepared by Squirrel Ashcraft. I don't know that this is worth photostating at 10 cents a page or whatever we pay. Yes, yes. It might be. If it is, we'll have that done. We could have it done this week. Otherwise, I'll make notes of anything important. No, let's do that. Let's do that. And then other notes which wouldn't do at all do photostat, which are so sketchy. And I dictated these to Lee Smith, who naturally hearing it verbally misspelled half of the names of musicians, which we still do. We still don't know the right spelling of a lot of these people. But she did the fine job. And I took down shorthand from when I'd talked to her. I would go to Chicago, of course, on these trips with the shadow players when we were working on the Jazzmen. And I'd interview all these fellows and make very sketchy notes in longhand. And I'd go back and try to remember exactly what they said or as much as I could what they said. And tell them to her, the various and large on the notes. And then she would try to write them down. And she, of course, there's a chance for errors three or four places there. But I'll go over the notes from people such as Clarence Williams. I have about four pages on Clarence Williams, who's since then had some very bad strokes. And probably will never be interviewed again. I don't believe Dick Allen got to see him. I don't even remember the details.
There's also a lot of material there that's invaluable. And we ought to be sure and get recorded some way.
Yes, that's why I'm making notes on the tape so that you'll know you'll get something from the people. I'll get something about Clarence Williams, which was done in New York.
Mrs. Rankin's supposed to keep after me.

Keep after me. But I've made notes also of the ones that I will send. I have a big sheet. I see. The Clarence Williams notes are especially in very bad shape. But I'll try to enlarge a little bit and correct what is here. And send those. Another man who's dead. Clarence Williams isn't dead, but unfortunately is in very bad health. Richard M. Jones died about 1946 in January, I believe. And I'd interviewed him a couple of times and have fairly good interviews. He was a very important figure in the Chicago scene. I think that was the right.
If you want to do it.

These notes, there are too many errors in it, which I can correct, I think, and do a better job by longhand, I believe, on this. And maybe enlarge a couple of things and leave out a few errors, too. Some of his information wasn't entirely accurate, but in general it was pretty good. He had a pretty good memory and was a very valuable source for a jazz man, a lot of the things that he told us. I know there are some bad errors, too, that he made.
Well, maybe you could correct him.

A footnote or something like that. Yes, sort of evaluate some of that, too. I'd rather do that and not take a lot of time on the tape now to do that. And they're not in a condition to be photostadded or Xerox or whatever it is. Another man who's dead now, Buddy Christian, an outstanding banjo and guitar player from New Orleans, who also played piano here and also in New York. And he played on quite a few of the Clarence Williams Hot Five. And what are they called? Blue Five, excuse me. Anyway, he's been dead for several years. I have very little notes on him, but at least a little bit about his life, which is very little known, the facts of his life. And I'll send that. Another man who's so very important because he's probably the oldest, maybe the oldest living jazz musician, if he is still living, Bill Johnson. I don't remember now if he's older than Papa Lane or not. It's pretty close, their age. But he was older than Bolden, for instance, I believe, a year or so. And you interviewed him in 38? No, in 38. He used to go to a little, I'll put that on since that doesn't tell you, a little, he was a waiter and sort of a cook in a little restaurant on 38th Street, right around the corner from the Union. He didn't belong to the Union, but he was working on Union jobs. The Union wasn't very important even in Chicago in 38. And that was in the middle of the Depression, almost the middle of the Depression yet. And he would work with Lil Armstrong and different people going up to Milwaukee and occasionally around Chicago. And I remember sitting there one whole afternoon with a whole lot of big jars of pigs' feet in front of me there, which I never did eat and I hope I never have to because I never did smell good. But I mean, he was running a sandwich shop in the back end of a saloon. That's what it was. He was really the cook and the waiter for the sandwich shop. And I don't remember what else they sold there, chitlings maybe and a few other things he'd cook up. But I went to his home and we got several very good pictures that were used in Jazzmen, a little card of the original Creole band. And he told me where the other members were. Almost all the members of that band except Freddie Keppert at that time were living. Even George Baquet. His George Baquet interview I must add to this list, which I didn't find there today. I have it someplace at home. I know where it is now. But I saw him in Philadelphia then. After the book Jazzmen was published, I interviewed him on the way to Pittsburgh after I left New York. But Bill Johnson, on account of his age, and he had a pretty good memory at that time, was a wonderful contact, but we still had very poor notes from him, about a page and two thirds, unfortunately. I might have a few pages. I met his wife also in California when I was there in 1940. And we tried to contact him. He left his old trunk in the basement of the place he lived. It was really next door, I believe. I went back there in 1958 after we got the grant to try to find him. And they said he was down in Mexico. I knew that he'd traveled to Texas and Mexico. I'd heard that from other friends through those years. Back and forth, he'd go down there for the winter. But they tore down the house he lived in, the trunk was stored next door. And this friend gave me his address. I wrote to him, no answer. And I'd write back to my friend, said, you must have given me the wrong address. No letter came back. Not known here. So he said, well, he's moved on to another little town. I think Marble Falls or Marble Head or something in Texas, a little town near San Antonio. Marble Falls. Marble Falls. Marble Falls. Tried to write to him there. No luck at all. And finally, Al Rose, whom you met and has been very helpful at times in our project, was traveling around making his cartoons in colleges and was in Texas and said he'd try to find him. I gave him all the dope I had. And he couldn't find him either. And his wife, Mary, who he says has good intuition, figured out maybe he's trying to pass for white. He was very light. He looked white. Always did. Very light. So that turned out to be the case. We found out a couple years later, he would pick up his mail at the Hilton Hotel in San Antonio. Evidently somebody worked there and he'd go there and pick up his mail there. A fellow from France who was writing supposedly a book on the original Creole band, it would be a small book I imagine, and what happened to the musicians, finally did contact him. He wasn't afraid of being found out that he was white. But he wouldn't answer a New Orleans letter, of course. And this fellow talked to him three or four times. He would drive out to the airport once with him. I think he had a car. But he said his memory was so bad, it was just almost hopeless to get any material.
Very old.

Very old. He was 90 then. That was about two years ago, 1960 or so. Maybe 1959 that I talked to this fellow from France. I have some notes on it, I couldn't find him today. But I'll also find those notes and add them to this Bill Johnson interview. I will take a practice trying to find him. I would have gone, I would have gambled some of our Tulane money as I said, which is expensive. I would have paid $50 for an interview. If I would both offer him $25 or $50 expenses gone out there, I would have done that. I would have gone at that time. But I don't believe it would be worth it now to try to find him. And there's a good chance he's dead at this time. That was two years or more ago. I doubt that we could find him. But if there's any way that you would ever find him, it would be still good to meet him. I don't think we'd get enough information to make it worthwhile.
I don't suppose he would have any written material or pictures of anything like that?

No, he had good pictures at that time. I was hoping to get some of those pictures, which I didn't copy all of them. They had pictures of Big Eye, Louie, and people. I remember one in the boxing match of Big Eye and Freddie Keppert outside the theater. They had their fists up as if they were boxing. A few other good pictures, which I didn't, it cost too much to reproduce them, I guess, at the time. The Jazzman, I didn't see all of them at that time either. But in 1940 or 41, on the way back from California about that time, I stopped and saw him for the last time. He was in the same apartment on South Parkway and had these pictures, which I'd hoped to get.
This is a valuable document, isn't it? This document.

Yes, it's very, very messy. About the best word I can say, both in the, we had no recording way to record it word for word. But it's the only contact. It must be a little bit better dope on here than the Frenchman got, unfortunately. It must be an arrangement for dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear He's a great talker, too. He's a great talker, and he may spread it on a little bit sometime. I'm not trying to knock him. He's got a good, he's got the gift of gab, you might say, more than most musicians, which is what Johnny Dodds always called it, the gift of gab. Johnny complained because he didn't have the gift of gab and wasn't a good talker at all. Oh, there's some Johnny Dodds notes. Let me put that on here, too, which are in another box.
Let me ask you about the Bill Johnson. You must have mentioned that to Don Alba, huh?

Yes, he's never heard of it. He didn't know he was in San Antonio. So Don, of course, is light enough to pass, too. He wouldn't have to be afraid to talk to Don, but he's passing, evidently. But with that age and his memory gone, evidently.
Is he kind of brown?
Pardon me?
Is he kind of brown? No, he's just... Lots of Mexicans, you know, are kind of dark. No, he's just light.

Light, of course, I have one. My skin is like baby skin. You can't say anybody's as white as me, but he's just as light as you are, actually, just about, really. Oh, thank you. He's very light. And his brother Dink was a little bit darker. But you know Don, Don Alba looks white, wouldn't you say? Pretty much so.
Yeah, he looks... His daughter, he has a daughter about nine or ten, and he's a little lighter.

Yeah, it's surprising. A couple more generations, they'll be faded out completely. Yeah. Another interview I have here, which is these longhand things are in pitiful shape as far as being word for word, is Paul Norez. I used to go to see him when he had a little barbecue place up on North State Street, about 800 block. Specialized in a secret formulae claimed of barbecue sauce. He was probably a pretty good cook though, and still a good trumpet player. Had sessions there on Monday nights of all the New Orleans musicians, whoever was there, like the Bob Crosby band, say if Zola or Johnny Dodds, he'd have Johnny and Baby come in quite often. Had some very good sessions. I only heard maybe one or two, I don't know if I heard more than one that I can say for sure, but he wasn't a great talker, but he still knew a lot of the fellows and had a lot to say on New Orleans music. I have only a page and a half of his here too.
Mr. Russell, I would like to take all of these and Xerox them. I'll have them typed as like they are and regard them as rough drafts. So if anything happened to you, we at least have them.
All right, if you want to do it, I'm certainly-
And then when you get the revision fixed up, well, we can substitute them.
I should have time up in Missouri.
Well, we'll arrange all that. If you just let me have them, I'll have them copied one way or the other. Now, this won't Xerox.

For instance, on the Paul Norez, if somebody has scratched out with a red pencil certain things and put X's as if they use certain paragraphs and certain ones, I don't think it doesn't mean that that isn't any more reliable than the other. It's just somebody was trying to-
Why don't you just give me all of these and I'll have them copied. All right, if you'd like to do- And we'll send you the original and a working copy.

Some of them are so short, it's pitiful. I'm ashamed of them, you know. It's all right. I'd go there and I'd talk maybe for a half an hour and then Lee Smith would take down my- I may have those others over there. Shorthand.
This will make it easier for you to work with them and make certain we've got some copies.
It may run into sort of an expense. What about the Defender notes done in longhand? I'd like to type them up.
They're awfully long.
It's gonna-
I'm not so sure. I think that was Xerox. I think it would too.
Yeah. Here are some other notes that Walter Allen took also about Joe Oliver. He was writing a book on Joe Oliver. He went there-
Now these are typed in the back of the Defender notes.

Yeah. That's some of the later Defender notes, some things that I probably didn't get. He probably looked through my notes and then went up there and went through a couple of years. We'll copy all this stuff for you. So in any case, there are a few other interviews, people that are dead there like Tubby Hall and Joe Lindsay. Unfortunately, we got very little bit from Tubby Hall. I wanted to apologize on that. He was one of the great drummers, I'm convinced the more I hear of other drummers especially. At that time, I probably didn't pay too much attention to him. I first heard him, oh, maybe half a dozen times on the south side with Johnny Dodd's band. And he wasn't spectacular at all. He just sat there and hardly moved. The one remark that Johnny made, I probably said, well, he's the one who was on the left. He probably said, well, he's the one who was on the Louis Armstrong records. Is that right or something? I wouldn't have hardly known who he was at that time when Johnny first introduced me. And Johnny said, yes, he doesn't, he started it confidentially. He doesn't play as much drums as he used to, you know. So I thought, well, he's not so good or not very great really. And I was more interested in Baby in those days. But then you talk later to Baby and find out Baby admits he got his press role mostly from Tubby Hall. And Tubby went up there, oh, three or four years before most of them, or maybe a couple of years before a lot of the other New Orleans. But he invented it? No, not necessarily. He was one of the first ones that had a good press role, though. But Tubby, I think, went up maybe as, say, something like Natty went up as a cigar maker. He went up as another job, not as a musician at first. He was there a year or so before Oliver and some of the other fellows. But he was undoubtedly one of the great drummers down here even, especially in Chicago, and had a wonderful, simple style. But it wasn't spectacular, and his Baby didn't run around on all the traps. And that one remark, I guess, that Johnny made to me, which Johnny wasn't really trying to knock him. He was just saying he maybe wasn't playing quite the drums he did maybe 10 years before or sometime, or 20 years before. But he was still great. And his brother was one of the great drummers with Kid Ori's band, too. That was the greatest rhythm section I ever heard, I'd say, was that Kid Ori rhythm section with, who's the bass player? Eddie Garland and Bud Scott and Minor Hall, who was the younger brother of Tubby Hall. I guess that's right. I have to stop and think.
Is Minor Hall still playing?
Yeah, no, Minor died. We got a good interview with him in 1958. Wow. He was playing very little then. He had left the Ori band in a disagreement.
I have a record he made with Joe Dierensburg. He might have played a little bit after that, not much.

So, because he, I heard. The LARP record? Yeah. It was made about that time, actually. He had cancer, I heard, at that time. He looked in pretty good health and talked like he'd be playing, like he was alright. But a couple years later, maybe about two years ago, he died. So, evidently he did have cancer. And he was one of the better drummers, not flashy in any way either. And maybe in some sense, monotonous compared to some of the other New Orleans drummers, but still a wonderful rhythm section. Buster Wilson was the other member of that section, which was easily the best I ever heard. Really terrific. So, I'll send some of these and go over the ones that you don't, that I don't have here, like George Bakke and Johnny Dodds notes. I have another interview someplace of Jimmy Noon. We did at that time, too. It's very difficult to get anybody down here that can tell anything about him at all. There's conflicting stories. But I'll send the dope that we got directly from him, which isn't as good as a real interview because it's, it went through me and then through Lee Smith and then done longhand. It's very sketchy. So, I think that finishes up what I had to say about preparing Jazzman, which incidentally has just hundreds and hundreds of errors in. Maybe not, maybe not quite the proportion, let's say a little red back book. By whom? You know, the Sam Charter's book, which has an unusual number of errors and misspellings in, which was done maybe 15 years later. It should have had less maybe, but I'm not trying to make excuses for the Jazzman, which is so far from perfect. We always should have gone back and revised it. But there's just a terrific amount of errors and things in there. Right now, speaking of errors, we still don't know much about Buddy Bolden, for instance. I remember one time speaking of Sam, since he brought in the name, about maybe as long as three years ago, he served notice on me.
